tokyo_dome_rules_and_restriction_researc.purpose: The 2026-08 high-rigor research gate for the proposed pre-Tokyo-Dome Japanese OCG snapshot: (1) what restriction list applied to Japanese OCG play immediately before/at the August 26, 1999 Tokyo Dome event, and (2) what game rules were actually in force there, and whether current EDOPro/ocgcore architecture can represent them. This section is RESEARCH ONLY - no canonical Tokyo Dome format, banlist, pool, or rule profile was created. Green tests are necessary but not proof of historical truth; several findings below sharpen or actively CONTRADICT the prior gate's working hypotheses rather than confirming them.

Agent B - Tokyo Dome event-document specialist
Agent C - early OCG rules chronology specialist
Agent D - ocgcore / EDOPro representability specialist (took A/B/C's candidate rules as input, did not research history independently)
Agent E - adversarial historical auditor (stress-tested A-D's strongest claims, did independent verification, found NEW problems A-D missed)

swarm.method: A, B, C ran in parallel with no cross-visibility. D consumed A/B/C's candidate rules only (no independent historical research). E consumed A/B/C/D's reports and independently re-verified specific claims (live Yugipedia revision-history API pulls, direct re-fetch of already-cited repo sources, direct schema/code reads) rather than merely critiquing prose. F (this section) resolves disagreements using the evidence hierarchy: (1) contemporaneous official Konami tournament/rule material, (2) contemporaneous official/publisher guidebooks or archived official pages, (3) later official Konami historical database material, (4) high-quality period scans/transcriptions with traceable provenance, (5) specialist historical community research, (6) generic wikis/unsourced lists - never by vote.

All engine-representability conclusions below are static analysis of docs/research/ocgcore-flags.md plus the ALREADY-EXISTING, ALREADY-RUN tests/engine/test_tokyo_dome_rules.py experiment (recorded in this packet's own phase_experiment block); no new engine test was added or run in this pass because pinned ocgcore was unavailable, and this is reported honestly rather than implied otherwise.

format_identity.snapshot_rationale: The task's instruction was to reassess the pre-event snapshot only if evidence proves the historically meaningful playable snapshot should instead be event-day and include same-day cards. This swarm found no such evidence; if anything it found evidence CUTTING AGAINST event-day cleanliness: (1) Agent B/E independently found multiple convergent-but-hedge-heavy retrospective sources (5+ independent Japanese blogs beyond what Agent B alone found) describing the event as disrupted by overcrowding severe enough to require riot police, with a live claim that the finals tournament itself may not have concluded at the venue that day and were possibly re-held regionally later - zero primary/contemporaneous (period newspaper, Konami statement) confirmation was found either way, by either agent, despite deliberate searching. (2) Directly verified against live repo state this session (not merely asserted): Gate Guardian, the events own headline attendance promo card, is ABSENT from the certified 370-card pre-event pool - and so are all three of its Fusion Material monsters (Suijin, Kazejin, Sanga of the Thunder), confirmed by recomputing retroformats.releases.evaluate_cutoff against the certified 1999-08-25 cutoff and checking all four names directly (none present in the 370). This means Gate Guardian could not have been Fusion Summoned by anyone restricted to the certified pre-event pool, regardless of exactly when its materials were later released. Cross-referenced (medium confidence, multi-source WebSearch corroboration since a direct Konami-database fetch could not complete in this sandbox - see source_bibliography) against community card-list aggregators converging on Vol.5, 1999-09-23 as the materials actual first OCG-JP release, a full month after Tokyo Dome - consistent with, though not required to support, the repo-verified absence finding. Both findings make 'the format played that day' a more fragile historical anchor than the pre-event certified-release-ledger snapshot, which rests on the repo's own independently re-verified, twice-audited (recertified commit 334f5865) product chronology. The pre-event 1999-08-25, 370-card snapshot remains the recommended and safer choice.
event_completion_caveat: NEW, significant finding not present in the prior gate: whether the Tokyo Dome tournament final actually concluded at the venue on August 26, 1999 as commonly assumed is itself in genuine doubt per multiple independent (but all retrospective, hedge-heavy, oral-history-based) Japanese community sources describing a crowd-control failure, riot police, cancelled Premium Pack sales, and a claim the finals never took place / were re-held regionally. No period (1999) documentary source was located by either Agent B or Agent E despite dedicated searching in both English and Japanese. This does not change the certified pre-event 370-card pool (which does not depend on the event concluding) but is material to any future claim that 'the Tokyo Dome format' represents a coherent, completed, single-day competitive event - it may represent a competitive structure that was announced and partially run, not one that cleanly concluded. Reported as an open historical question, not resolved either way.

july_1999_fabrication_trace.claim_examined: Various community sources describe a 'July 1999' Japanese restriction list preceding Tokyo Dome.
july_1999_fabrication_trace.finding: Agent A traced the 'July 1999' date on Yugipedia's restricted-list history page to a specific 2017 edit (identified via the MediaWiki revisions API, action=query&prop=revisions) that introduced the date with a citation to a source that, on direct re-read, does NOT state a July date anywhere - it is undated. Agent E independently re-pulled the same revision history and confirmed the citation mismatch. Neither agent found any 1999-dated primary document naming a specific July release. The '1999-07' working_id already present in this packet from a prior session is therefore UNSUPPORTED by primary evidence and should be treated as a placeholder, not a finding - this is a correction to the prior gate's own framing, not new fabrication.
july_1999_fabrication_trace.disposition: The working_id 'ocg-1999-07' in the existing banlist.working_id field should be read as provisional/unverified going forward; no better-evidenced date was found for the restriction list's own effective/publication date, only for its CONTENT.

scope_dispute.finding: NEW in this pass (found by Agent E, not surfaced by A/B/C): the two sources this packet already cites for the 3-card restriction list - Yugipedia and ocg-card.com - describe DIFFERENT OBJECTS when read closely. Yugipedia's page frames the 3-card list as Konami's first OFFICIAL nationwide restriction list, implicitly applicable to all sanctioned OCG play. ocg-card.com's page (an independent Japanese cataloguing site, not Konami) frames what looks like the same 3 cards as a TOURNAMENT-SPECIFIC rule sheet tied to a named 1999 regional/qualifying event, not a blanket nationwide restriction. Neither page cites a Konami-original document; both are downstream retrospectives. This produces a genuine three-way ambiguity: (a) nationwide official restriction list in force for ALL Japanese OCG play by Aug 1999, (b) a tournament-specific ruleset for one or more qualifying events that may or may not have applied at Tokyo Dome itself, (c) a modern community retro-format convention retrofitted onto 1999 with no 1999-dated basis at all. The swarm could not adjudicate between these three readings - no source examined states which one is correct, and no contemporaneous (1999) Konami document was located by any agent.
scope_dispute.adjudication: Applying the evidence hierarchy: both cited sources sit at tier 5-6 (specialist community research / semi-generic wiki), well below the tier-1/2 contemporaneous-official material the hierarchy prioritizes. Since the two available tier-5/6 sources actively disagree on SCOPE (not just on details within a shared scope), the hierarchy gives no basis to prefer one over the other - this is a genuine evidentiary tie at the lowest tiers, not a case where a higher-tier source resolves a lower-tier disagreement. Per the task's explicit instruction ('if evidence can't support an exact complete list, do NOT invent one - mark canonicalization BLOCKED' and 'model ordinary-OCG-restrictions vs Tokyo-Dome-tournament-restrictions vs later-retro-format-community-convention SEPARATELY if they differ'), this is exactly that condition: the three readings differ in ways that matter (nationwide legal restriction vs one-event tournament rule vs modern retrofit) and cannot be collapsed into one list without guessing which the sources meant.

restriction_list_research.verdict_detail: Restriction-list CONTENT (Raigeki/Dark Hole/Trap Hole, Limited-to-1, single-tier) is well-corroborated across independent sources and is NOT in dispute. Restriction-list SCOPE (nationwide-OCG vs Tokyo-Dome-tournament-only vs modern-retrofit) IS in dispute between the two best available sources and cannot be resolved with currently available evidence. Canonicalization of a restriction list for this format is therefore BLOCKED per the task's explicit instruction, pending discovery of a contemporaneous (tier 1-3) source that states which of the three scopes is correct.

rule_chronology.method: Agent C built this by walking the Japanese rulebook lineage from the original 1999 Starter Box rulebook forward through the 'Expert Rules' transition, cross-checked by Agent E against independent rulebook-scan community archives. Per the task's suspicion requirement, Agent C and Agent E both explicitly flagged and discounted retrospective sources that collapse multiple distinct 1999 rule revisions into a single undifferentiated 'old rules' bucket.

classified_rules.rationale: DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 is the only related flag. It removes the Main Phase 2 window entirely, which happens to match '1999 had no Main Phase 2' at a surface level, but the already-run test_tokyo_dome_rules.py experiment found DUEL_NO_MAIN_PHASE_2 also removes a distinct post-battle legal action window the actual 1999 single-Main-Phase model never had to begin with (period rules allowed certain post-battle actions inside the single Main Phase's continuation, not a discrete second phase) - so the flag changes MORE than the history requires in one direction while getting the headline behavior right in another. Classified as approximated, not exact, and this gap was already flagged in this packet's existing architecture.gaps before this pass; this pass CONFIRMS rather than newly discovers it.

DUEL_ATTACK_FIRST_TURN's companion no-draw-on-first-turn behavior is a direct flag-level match already exercised in tests/engine/test_historical_behaviour.py per the harness constants read this session.

DUEL_ATTACK_FIRST_TURN exists and can toggle this at the engine level, so the ENGINE side is exactly representable either way - but rule_chronology above found the historical fact itself (was first-turn attack legal at the Aug 25/26 1999 boundary) is unresolved between agents. Classification therefore tracks the historical unknown, not an engine limitation.

event_day_pool_interaction.finding: No source located by Agent B, Agent C, or Agent E establishes that any Aug-26-distributed card was legal for use IN tournament decks played that same day, as opposed to being a souvenir/take-home item distributed at or after the event concluded. The Gate Guardian promo specifically is affirmatively evidenced to have been UNUSABLE in any coherent deck at the event, since its Fusion Material monsters were not released until Sept 23, 1999 (Vol.5) - a full month later. This is strong (though indirect) evidence AGAINST the 'released at the event = legal in the event' assumption in at least this one headline case, and no evidence was found supporting that assumption for any other Aug 26 product either.
event_day_pool_interaction.conclusion: Per the task's explicit instruction not to infer 'released at the event' = 'legal in the event' absent proof, and given the affirmative Gate Guardian counter-evidence, the pre-event 1999-08-25 370-card pool is CONFIRMED as the safer and better-evidenced recommendation. No Aug 26 product is added to the pool by this research pass.
